Family Health

Food cravings before a period: respond without guilt

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Wanting chocolate, crisps or a larger meal before a period is not a failure of self-control. Notice what helps you feel nourished and comfortable, while paying attention to distress, loss-of-control eating or symptoms that disrupt everyday life.

Appetite changes can follow a menstrual pattern

Feeling hungrier or wanting particular foods before a period is common. Some people notice it in the final seven to ten days before bleeding, while others notice a broader or less predictable pattern in the one or two weeks beforehand. Cravings may ease after bleeding begins. There is no exact timetable that every cycle must follow.

Other premenstrual changes can include bloating, headaches, spots, breast tenderness, tiredness and shifts in mood. Bowel habits or gas may also change around this time. Looking at several symptoms together is more informative than treating a single desire for chocolate as a diagnostic sign. Symptoms that continue throughout the month may need another or an additional explanation.

Hormones may contribute, but research is not a simple formula

Changing ovarian hormones are one possible influence on appetite and cravings. A small 2016 study followed seventeen people with regular menstrual cycles, measuring hormones and asking about foods they craved. It found relationships involving estradiol, sex hormone-binding globulin and leptin, including patterns of stronger sweet and carbohydrate cravings. The findings suggest a biological contribution but do not prove a universal cause.

The study does not show that everyone needs a particular food when estrogen or progesterone reaches a certain level. Sleep, stress, familiar foods, access and whether you have eaten enough also affect appetite. Ordinary cravings do not diagnose a hormone imbalance or identify an exact missing nutrient. Testing or supplements should be based on a relevant clinical concern, not a craving alone.

Food and mood interact without a guaranteed chemical boost

Eating something enjoyable can be comforting, especially when you feel tired, irritable or low. Carbohydrates and brain chemistry, including serotonin pathways, have been studied in relation to mood. However, the claim that a sweet food reliably releases a “happiness chemical” and fixes premenstrual distress is too simple. A short-lived change in how you feel is not treatment for persistent depression or anxiety.

You do not need to feel guilty for enjoying food or expect it to meet every emotional need. Notice whether eating helps you feel nourished and satisfied, or whether it has become the only available way to cope. That observation can guide support without labelling foods as good or bad or blaming yourself for wanting relief.

Respond to hunger with enough, reasonably regular food

Appetite and energy needs can vary across the cycle, but there is no single extra-calorie allowance that every person must add before a period. If you feel hungry, eating a satisfying meal or snack is reasonable. Skipping the next meal to compensate can leave you hungrier and make the cycle more difficult.

Include foods you enjoy alongside carbohydrate, protein, fat and fibre across the day. Examples might be rice and beans, toast with eggs, or yogurt with fruit and nuts. If you have a medical meal plan, ask how to accommodate changes in hunger within it. A registered dietitian can help if nutrition advice has become confusing, restrictive or difficult to put into practice.

Carbohydrate choices can support comfort and variety

Bread, pasta and potatoes are not inherently unsuitable foods before a period. Whole grains and pulses, such as brown rice, oats, beans and lentils, can add fibre and help make a meal satisfying. They are options within ordinary eating, not a guaranteed way to keep serotonin high. You can choose a portion that leaves you comfortable rather than trying to follow a rigid rule.

Spaghetti squash can be an enjoyable vegetable in a favourite pasta-style dish, but being lower in calories or carbohydrate does not make it a necessary replacement for pasta. Use it because you like it, and make sure the meal still provides enough nourishment. If large meals or very salty foods seem to worsen bloating, experiment gently with timing or amounts instead of banning an entire food group.

Make room for sweet foods and chocolate

Sweet snacks can fit into a varied diet. If you want alternatives or additions, possibilities include a smoothie, yogurt and fruit, apple with a little honey, a homemade oat-and-nut snack, or a fruit-and-nut mix. These are choices, not compulsory substitutes for a biscuit or dessert. Pairing a snack with something filling may help if a small sweet item leaves you hungry.

Chocolate is a frequently reported craving. Dark chocolate contains cocoa compounds and some minerals, but that does not make it a proven PMS treatment or mean a craving diagnoses magnesium deficiency. You do not have to choose the darkest bar or stop after an arbitrary number of squares. Consider enjoyment, satisfaction and any symptoms you personally notice, without treating a food as a prescription.

Broaden the ways you get comfort

A walk, a run if you enjoy running, a funny film, a conversation with a friend or time with a pet may help you feel supported or more settled. Consensual intimacy can be enjoyable if you want it, but it is not an obligation or a treatment requirement. Rest can be the more useful choice on a difficult day.

These activities should not become a way to earn food or burn off a snack. Their effects cannot be reduced to a guaranteed dose of endorphins, serotonin, oxytocin or dopamine. Choose what feels manageable, and seek support when sadness, anxiety or irritability are strong enough to disrupt your relationships, work, study or ordinary routines.

Distinguish cravings, binge eating and PMDD

Eating more than usual is not automatically binge eating. Repeated episodes of feeling unable to stop, eating in secrecy, marked distress, or attempts to compensate through vomiting, fasting or excessive exercise deserve professional attention. Support is appropriate at any body size; a significant weight change is not a requirement for care. Restrictive dieting can make loss-of-control eating harder to manage.

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD, involves a broader pattern of severe cyclical symptoms, particularly mood symptoms, that interfere with life. Appetite changes may be part of it, but cravings alone do not establish the diagnosis. A clinician may use daily symptom records across at least two cycles. Treatment can include psychological support or medicines; you do not have to manage severe symptoms through food choices alone.

Irregular periods and pregnancy need their own consideration

Research has found an association between binge eating and menstrual dysfunction. For example, a study of 11,503 Swedish women examined those experiences together. It does not prove that an irregular period causes binge eating, or that a particular percentage applies to everyone. Shared hormonal, metabolic or other factors may contribute. Mention both menstrual changes and distressing eating to a clinician rather than assuming one explains the other.

Cravings, nausea, food aversions and breast or nipple changes cannot reliably distinguish pregnancy from PMS. A missed period is a reason to consider a test if pregnancy is possible. Most tests can be used from the first day of a missed period; if you do not know when the next period is due, test at least twenty-one days after unprotected sex. If an early result is negative but concern remains, repeat as instructed or seek advice.

Ask for help with persistent distress or non-food cravings

Arrange a review if hunger or cravings are new, persist all month, interfere with daily life, cause significant distress or affect recovery from an eating disorder. Also mention ongoing depression, anxiety, major weight changes or other physical symptoms. A brief record of timing, mood, sleep and eating can help; use a gentler approach if tracking makes you more anxious or obsessive.

Wanting to eat clay, soil, paper or other non-food substances, or repeatedly craving ice, deserves assessment. This may be pica and can be associated with iron deficiency, particularly with heavy periods, but it is not a diagnosis by itself. Do not eat potentially harmful substances or start high-dose iron on your own. Seek urgent help if you have swallowed something toxic or feel at risk of harming yourself; a symptom diary can wait.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Premenstrual guidance recognises appetite changes and recommends help when symptoms affect daily life.

Hormone and menstrual-function studies show associations, not a personal diagnosis or a rule about which foods you must eat.

How BeMama can help

Choose a few accessible meals and snacks before the days that are usually harder. Record symptom timing only if it helps rather than adding pressure.

When to seek help

Seek support for loss-of-control eating, compensatory behaviours, persistent mood symptoms or non-food cravings. Immediate risk of self-harm or ingestion of a toxic substance requires urgent help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Appetite may change without following an exact schedule.
  • A craving is not a hormone or nutrient test.
  • Regular, sufficient eating is more useful than compensation.
  • Comfort can include both food and other enjoyable activities.
  • Distressing eating or severe cyclical mood symptoms deserve care.

Frequently asked questions

When do premenstrual cravings usually begin?

Some people notice them in the final seven to ten days before bleeding; others have symptoms across the preceding one or two weeks. The pattern varies, and cravings may ease after the period starts.

Did the 2016 study prove hormones cause every craving?

No. It studied seventeen participants and found associations between hormone-related measures and cravings. It did not establish a universal cause, a personal hormone imbalance or a required food choice.

Does craving chocolate mean I need magnesium?

Not reliably. A food craving cannot identify a nutrient deficiency. Chocolate can be enjoyed as food, but it is not a diagnostic test or a proven treatment for PMS.

Should I replace all pasta and bread before my period?

No. Those foods can be part of normal eating. Wholegrain options and pulses can add fibre, and vegetables can add variety, but a lower-calorie substitute is not automatically a better response to hunger.

Is it wrong to want sweet foods?

No. You can include foods you enjoy without guilt. If a snack leaves you hungry, add something more filling. Seek support if eating feels repeatedly out of control or causes significant distress.

Does eating more mean I have binge eating disorder?

No. A larger appetite or meal alone does not establish that diagnosis. Recurrent loss of control and distress deserve assessment, regardless of body size or weight change.

Can cravings diagnose PMDD?

No. PMDD involves a broader cyclical pattern with severe mood symptoms and disruption of daily life. Appetite changes can occur, but a clinician assesses the complete pattern.

Do irregular periods cause binge eating?

Research shows an association, not proof of a one-way cause. Hormonal, metabolic and other factors may overlap. It is useful to discuss both concerns rather than treating one as an explanation for the other.

Can cravings or food aversions tell me I am pregnant?

No. Symptoms overlap. Use a correctly timed pregnancy test when pregnancy is possible, and repeat or seek advice if an early negative result does not fit what happens next.

What if I crave ice, soil or paper?

Persistent non-food cravings or repeated ice craving should be discussed with a clinician. Iron deficiency is one possible association, especially with heavy periods, but testing and an individual treatment plan are needed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
